title: I made my first very rough fishing game with Claude — should I continue?
author: SeaworthinessFit6280
selftext:
Hi everyone,  
I made my first very rough demo of a fishing game with the full help of Claude. I don’t know how to code at all.  
I uploaded it to [itch.io](http://itch.io/). If anyone has time to try it, I would really appreciate your honest opinion. Should I continue working on it or give up?  
If I should continue, could you also give me some advice on how to use Claude more efficiently? I have a Claude Pro subscription, but I reach the limit very quickly.  
[https://kholodniuk.itch.io/fishing-nostalgy](https://kholodniuk.itch.io/fishing-nostalgy)  
Thanks!

comments.author: InSilicoAwards
comments.body: I would have it localize in English also, not sure if you did, but I didn't see a way to flip text. It's trivial with machine tools now.

comments.author: StellarAmazoniansDev
comments.body: It looks really good, and—odd as it may seem—there are a lot of people interested in fishing simulators. That said, making an English version would be much better; sticking to Russian (or whatever language) limits you to just your own country.

replies.author: SeaworthinessFit6280
replies.body: Sorry , it is really my big fault ( it is Ukrainian ☺️)

comments.author: RUSuper
comments.body:
Line throw could be a little better, on top of the fact that I don't understand anything :D 

But maybe it can work as a mobile game tbh.

comments.author: V1_Bau
comments.body:
I’m a game producer and I just played your demo. Whether this project should continue isn't a matter of how to leverage Claude or Codex, it’s about getting a clear grasp on player demand and the competitive landscape first. Can you answer these three questions for yourself?

1. How has the history of fishing games evolved? How have player needs shifted alongside the genre's evolution?

2. What are the top 3 games in the fishing genre? What are their strengths, weaknesses, and unique selling points? 

3. Why do players play virtual fishing games instead of grabbing a rod and going to a real lake? What core experience  are they actually chasing?

There are plenty of other questions, but if you can get clarity on these three first, then we can talk about whether this demo is worth pursuing further.

replies.author: SeaworthinessFit6280
replies.body:
Thank you,   
I really appreciate this comment. You’re right — I was focusing too much on how to build the game with AI instead of first asking why players would want to play it at all.   
  
Your three questions are very useful, and I’m going to think about them properly. My current idea is that \*Fishing Nostalgia\* should not try to compete with the biggest fishing simulators in realism or complexity. I want it to focus more on atmosphere, relaxation, nature, nostalgia and simple progression. One thing I also want to explore is a stronger European fishing identity. From what I’ve seen, many popular fishing games are built around a broader or more American-style fishing experience. I’d like my game to feel more familiar to European anglers — with European fish species, tackle, locations and the general atmosphere of fishing here. But I agree that I need to understand the market and player expectations much better before deciding whether this direction really makes sense. Thanks again for taking the time to play the demo and give such useful feedback. I really appreciate it.

comments.author: qing-turn
comments.body: On hitting the limit fast: what helped me most was keeping each conversation small. I keep one task file in the project that describes the game and what's left to do, then start a fresh session for each task and point it at that file. One huge chat that keeps rereading everything burns through the limit much faster.
